A 66-year-old Polish man has been charged with planning an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk as part of an attempt to overthrow the government. A search of his home revealed improvised explosive devices that he allegedly planned to use in the plot.

The suspect, who can be named only as Krzysztof N. under Polish privacy law, has also been charged with a number of other offences, including promoting a war of aggression in Ukraine and inciting hate crimes. Media reports have identified the man as a radical-right extremist.

Do Prokuratury Okręgowej w Warszawie został doprowadzony 66-letni Krzysztof N., zatrzymany w związku z planowaniem zamachu na @donaldtusk i @KosiniakKamysz ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/rjcR3rNvyW

— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 13, 2026

On Sunday, Poland’s security services announced that they had received what they described as “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Tusk and his defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

Later that day, a 66-year-old suspect was detained in the city of Wrocław, southwest Poland, and his property was searched. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński told broadcaster TVP that the man was “very active in groups promoting extreme views”.

On Tuesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw, where Krzysztof N. has been transported, announced that he had been charged with nine offences.

“The most serious charge is for planning to forcibly overthrow state authorities, including the prime minister and cabinet, using explosives,” said spokesman Piotr Antoni Skiba. That crime carries a potential prison sentence of up to 15 years.

 

Skiba revealed that “a dozen or so” improvised explosive devices, which appeared to be similar to fragmentation grenades, had been found in the man’s home. There was also a crossbow, sharp-tipped metal bolts, and what are believed to be blank-firing or pneumatic guns.

Skiba said that Krzysztof N.’s plans had been discovered after an anonymous person sent a message to the State Protection Service (SOP), which is responsible for the security of high-ranking officials, that included a recording of a conversation purportedly with the suspect.

Krzysztof N. could be heard claiming that he had gathered “sevel hundred people” who shared his ideological beliefs and would help him overthrown the Polish government by force.

At the moment, there is no indication that Krzysztof N. or the group around him were inspired in any way by foreign intelligence agencies, but the issue is still being investigated, added Skiba, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Poland’s security services say they have received “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz https://t.co/zl3vt6mah3

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 11, 2026

Among the other charges Krzysztof N. has heard are “promoting a war of aggression, including in Ukraine, as well as incitement to commit crimes based on nationality, ethnicity, race and political views”, added Skiba. The suspect has so far pleaded not guilty on all counts.

On Monday, Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading daily, reported that Krzysztof N. had for months been posting videos online calling on fellow right-wing extremists to fight against the authorities. He also expressed antisemitic and anti-Ukrainian sentiment.

Another newspaper, Rzeczpospolita, found that he runs a Facebook page called Radical Polish Resistance Movement that has almost 8,000 followers and claims Poland’s two main political parties – Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) – are “in the hands of globalists and Judeo-communists”.

"Patriota do przesady". Kim jest Krzysztof N., Wrocławianin podejrzewany przez służby o planowanie zamachu na premiera Tuska

Mężczyzna, który miał planować zamach na premiera Donalda Tuska Od kilku miesięcy nagrywał w mediach społecznościowych filmiki i skrzykiwał prawicowych…

— Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 12, 2026

In a separate case, government spokesman Adam Szłapka announced on Tuesday that a 46-year-old man in the town of Oborniki in western Poland had been detained on suspicion of publicly calling for the murder of Tusk and the speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty.

A spokeswoman for the district prosecutor’s office in Oborniki told PAP that the man had been charged with inciting murder, for which he could face up to three years in prison.

“He admitted to publishing content insulting various government officials, but denied the charge of inciting their murder,” she revealed. “He expressed regret and remorse.”

Warsaw and Oslo also pledged to work together on strengthening NATO’s eastern and northern flanks, as well as to coordinate responses to cyberattacks, hybrid operations and foreign information manipulation.

Data harvested from mobile phones by the Polish authorities using Pegasus spyware were transmitted outside Poland and were accessible to the tool’s Israeli producer, Polish prosecutors have revealed as part of an investigation into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence.

Tego o Pegasusie jeszcze nie słyszeliście. pic.twitter.com/etvhTE9EWa

— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026

Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures.

In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets, including a number of PiS’s political opponents.

Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance.

PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing.

 

After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW).

The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data.

“Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office.

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 12, 2026

The ABW experts also highlighted serious concerns over management and security of the harvested data, noting that Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA), which was responsible for using the spyware, “did not have full control over the Pegasus system”.

“The CBA did not have passwords to access some accounts with administrative privileges and some system components remained under the control of the manufacturer [NSO],” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The server module responsible for infecting mobile devices remained under the manufacturer’s exclusive control.”

Data transmitted through the Pegasus system travelled outside Polish territory, through “servers located in various parts of the world”, in a network managed by NSO and “beyond the CBA’s control”, found the experts.

Meanwhile, NSO “had technical access to materials from operational surveillance”, although prosecutors say that the experts “did not determine whether the manufacturer actually obtained access to materials from specific operations”.

Łukasz Gibała, an independent, has won the mayoral election in Kraków, Poland’s second-biggest city, beating Monika Piątkowska, the candidate backed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

With all votes counted by just after 1 a.m. on Monday morning, Gibała had 62.1% against 37.9% for Piątkowska, who had already conceded defeat shortly after 9 p.m. on Sunday night, when exit polls showed a large margin of victory for her opponent. Turnout was 44.3%.

“Today in Poland, more and more people realise that we don’t have to live in the reality that politicians in Warsaw project upon us,” declared Gibała as it became clear he had won. “More and more people realise that we, in our own towns and cities, know better what’s good for us than they do in Warsaw.”

Among her campaign promises were to seek to locate an AI “gigafactory” in Kraków, to boost the availability of housing for young people, and to implement a package of policies for women, including free mammograms, pram-friendly infrastructure, free menstrual hygiene products, and safer nighttime public transport.

Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb.

Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026

Kraków’s election was held in unusual circumstances after the previous mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, also from KO, was removed from his position in May, just two years into his term. He had faced accusations of cronyism and poor financial management, as well as criticism over the introduction of the clean transport zone.

A petition to hold a recall referendum received more than the 58,355 signatures required. In the subsequent referendum, 97.3% supported removing the mayor (Miszalski had appealed to his supporters not to vote in an unsuccessful effort to keep turnout below the 27% needed for the result to be binding).

Before today’s election, both Miszalski and Majchowski had called on Cracovians to vote for Piątkowska. After his victory had become clear, Gibała declared that “11 October 2026 will be remembered as the day when, after 24 years, the inhabitants of Krakow regained their city”.

The vote had been particularly closely watched as it came just a year before the parliamentary elections. Gibała’s victory has been celebrated by figures from the right-wing opposition, though the new mayor is not politically aligned with them (and indeed previously served as an MP in Tusk’s party).

Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar.

They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time.

Sąd Rejonowy w Wałbrzychu w najbliższym czasie zdecyduje o losie trójki obcokrajowców, którzy pod koniec zeszłego roku niezgodnie z polskim prawem ubili kozę. Oskarżająca Hindusa i dwójkę Bengalczyków…

— Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 7, 2026

The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.

After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.

The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF

 

A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.

However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.”

Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.

The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set.

However, the country has itself been experiencing growing levels of migration in recent years. Most of the new arrivals are from neighbouring Ukraine and Belarus, but there are also growing numbers from outside Europe, too.

Indians are now Poland’s third-largest immigrant group, numbering around 25,500, according to recent data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Among first residence permits issued by Poland last year, Indians (9,230) and Turks (7,533) were the fourth and fifth largest recipients.

Poland’s current government has blamed some immigrant groups for a rise in crime and has stepped up deportations of those found to have broken the law. However, data show that, overall, immigrants are less likely to commit crimes than Poles themselves.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Wed, 14 Oct 2026 17:14:03 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Benefits and pensions for foreign nationals ‘cost £23bn’ https://www.cityam.com/benefits-and-pensions-for-foreign-nationals-cost-23bn/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 16:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465951

Spending on benefits and pensions for foreign nationals totalled about £23bn in 2025, according to a leading think tank, amid calls for a rethink on the impcat of immigration and the welfare system.  The Centre for Social Justice estimated that the UK government spent about £23bn on benefits, pensions and child-related support for non-British nationals [...]]]>

Spending on benefits and pensions for foreign nationals totalled about £23bn in 2025, according to a leading think tank, amid calls for a rethink on the impcat of immigration and the welfare system. 

The Centre for Social Justice estimated that the UK government spent about £23bn on benefits, pensions and child-related support for non-British nationals last year. 

Research found that approximately £14.3bn of spending was for working-age benefits. The total bill could rise to almost £27bn by 2030, according to estimates. 

The Westminster think tank’s new report challenges assumptions on the effects of immigration for the UK economy and impacts of welfare spending. 

Researchers crunched data provided by the Department for Work and Pensions, HMRC and the Home Office and suggested that about 1.85m non-British nationals received at least one form of welfare support last year. Government officials said they did not recognise the CSJ’s estimates due to its use of samples. 

An estimated 400,000 foreign nationals also received the state pension, which is also projected to rise over the next few years. 

The CSJ said the rise in benefits claims had “accompanied the unprecedented rise in immigration seen in recent years”. UK net migration peaked at around 944,000 in the year to March 2023, making migration a key national issue. 

While most people on visas do not have recourse to public funds, access to the welfare system can be granted after migrants secure settled status, otherwise known as indefinite leave to remain. 

Home secretary Shabana Mahmood had planned to double the time after which most foreign nationals can apply for settled status from five to 10 years would apply retrospectively to people who arrived in the UK in 2021. Her stricter rules have led to backlash within Labour ranks, although both Tory and Reform leaders have pledged to go further in denying some foreign nationals from claiming benefits. 

Benefits system must ‘restore contribution’

Sir Ian Duncan Smith, the former Tory leader who founded the CSJ, called on the government to join up welfare policies with its approach on immigration. 

“At a time when families and businesses are being clobbered with yet more taxes, many will be deeply concerned at the extent to which governments have let unconstrained immigration drive up the welfare bill,” Duncan Smith said. 

“We must urgently now restore contribution and reciprocity to the welfare system while helping the millions of Brits on out-of-work benefits back towards a better future for themselves and their families.”

At Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday, Andy Burnham said he would “get the welfare bill down” although reforms may only come after the Budget. 

A government spokesperson said: “We do not recognise these figures, which appear to be based on small-sample survey data, which is not robust enough to produce reliable estimates.

“Under this government, net migration is down by 82 per cent from its 2023 peak, and only people with eligible immigration status can claim taxpayer-funded benefits, of which around half of those claiming Universal Credit are in work.

“We have also set out proposals which will double the standard qualifying period to 10 years for most migrants, with shorter routes for those who contribute most to the UK.”

]]> 2465951Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Khan climbdown: Palantir settles £50m Met row after fears of ‘unlawful’ bias https://www.cityam.com/khan-climbdown-palantir-settles-50m-met-row-after-fears-of-unlawful-bias/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 15:34:56 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465877

Palantir has settled its High Court battle with Sadiq Khan’s policing office over a blocked £50m Metropolitan Police contract, following concerns that the decision had been unlawfully influenced by the US tech giant’s values and ethics. City AM understands the company pursued legal action not only to challenge the decision, but also to make sure [...]]]>

Palantir has settled its High Court battle with Sadiq Khan’s policing office over a blocked £50m Metropolitan Police contract, following concerns that the decision had been unlawfully influenced by the US tech giant’s values and ethics.

City AM understands the company pursued legal action not only to challenge the decision, but also to make sure it would not face discrimination in future contracts and to repair any reputational damage caused.

The settlement, announced on Wednesday, sees both Palantir and the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime (MOPAC) withdraw their allegations, with the company welcomed back into the bidding process.

The dispute began in May, when MOPAC blocked a proposed two-year contract for Palantir to provide AI technology to help the Met automate criminal intelligence analysis.

Palantir argued that the decision had been influenced by political considerations, while MOPAC maintained that the Met had failed to follow proper procurement procedures.

In a joint statement, MOPAC insisted its decision was based on governance, affordability and value for money, rather than Palantir’s ethics.

“MOPAC is happy to correct any contrary impression”, the statement said.

The mayor’s office also confirmed it had never operated a policy against contracting with Palantir and that the company would be welcome to compete in the renewed procurement process.

Palantir re-enters the bidding process

Palantir senior vice president Tom Watson welcomed the settlement, saying the case had sought to establish whether public procurement rules were being applied fairly.

“The mayor and his team have recognised their actions could have created the impression that the decision to block the UOA contract was based on Palantir’s values”, he said.

He added that procurement decisions should be made on their merits, even in the face of pressure from campaign groups.

Khan also praised the company’s contribution to London, saying Palantir supported jobs and investment in the capital.

“Palantir makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital, employing a large number of Londoners whose services have been procured legally by organisations across the UK and beyond”, he said.

The settlement brings an end to proceedings that had been due for a full High Court hearing in January 2027.

Both parties will bear their own legal costs. Earlier court budgets had put their combined potential costs at more than £8m.

The Met has since begun a fresh procurement process for the AI technology, with MOPAC pledging that all bidders, including Palantir, will be treated fairly.

The settlement comes days after the Met revealed that Palantir’s existing technology had helped uncover misconduct by the head of its Special Constabulary.

]]> 2465877Saskia Koopman Saskia Koopman Banks of England chief economist ‘sceptical’ of markets’ interest rate expectations https://www.cityam.com/bank-of-england-pill-interest-rate-forecast/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 15:31:45 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465809

The Bank of England is unlikely to vote for the four interest-rate hikes forecast by financial markets, according to its chief economist, who added the central bank should have raised rates in the early stages of the Iran war. Huw Pill, who has the most hawkish track record on the Monetary Policy Committee, played down [...]]]>

The Bank of England is unlikely to vote for the four interest-rate hikes forecast by financial markets, according to its chief economist, who added the central bank should have raised rates in the early stages of the Iran war.

Huw Pill, who has the most hawkish track record on the Monetary Policy Committee, played down the chances of the Bank raising rates by a full percentage point in the next year – the current path implied by financial markets.

He told an International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok he was “sceptical” about the need for such a sharp monetary tightening even as the Iran war threatens to carry inflation above four per cent at the start of next year.

“To get 100 basis points [of rate rises], we need a concrete manifestation of these risks [to wages and prices],” Pill told reporters. “We will get more evidence in the next six to nine months on second-round effects.”

Traders can effectively bet on the Bank of England’s interest rate path via what are known as swap rates. Since the onset of the Middle East conflict, the swaps market has consistently overestimated the number of UK central bank rate hikes, and currently suggests the MPC will vote for four interest rate rises in the next 12 months.

Bank of England can’t rely on ‘hall of mirrors’ from natural tightening

But throughout the war, officials have so far left Bank Rate unchanged and are instead on high alert for signs of so-called ‘second round effects’. The pattern, where the price pressure from an initial shock becomes embedded in an economy via wage and price setting, has so far failed to materialise. Price rises have so far been largely restricted to energy and fuel.

Pill said that despite the absence of second-round effects to date, the spectre of a 20 per cent jump in energy bills next year meant the Bank should have voted for an interest rate hike at the start of the war to prove it was “active”.

“It would have been good to move early and influence market expectations, and send a clearer signal we were active and agile,” he said. “I don’t think we have been in a good place.”

Other rate-setters have pointed to the monetary tightening that has occurred organically from the Bank of England’s decision to leave interest rates unchanged rather than cut them. The change in tack brought about by the war has led banks and mortgage providers to increase the rates they charge on new borrowing. The average rate of a five-year mortgage has jumped above six per cent from an average rate of below five per cent before March.

But Pill, who has voted to raise rates at every meeting since the Iran war, warned the Bank could not continue to rely on the natural tightening, branding it a “hall of mirrors” that could become a “house of cards”. “Acting and being agile feels more comfortable to me,” he said, adding: “You are doing something you are controlling.”

]]> 2465809Ali Lyon Ali Lyon Sport media rights value defies worries to hit record $66bn in 2026 https://www.cityam.com/sport-media-rights-value-defies-worries-to-hit-record-66m-in-2026/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 15:15:36 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465916

Sports media rights values hit record levels this year and are forecast to continue defying warnings of the bubble bursting, according to a new report. The World Cup and bumper new agreements for the NBA and UFC drove the total aggregate value – the main revenue source for all major sports – from $62.4bn in [...]]]>

Sports media rights values hit record levels this year and are forecast to continue defying warnings of the bubble bursting, according to a new report.

The World Cup and bumper new agreements for the NBA and UFC drove the total aggregate value – the main revenue source for all major sports – from $62.4bn in 2024 to $65.8bn in 2026, the SportBusiness Global Media Report found.

It means the worldwide market has enjoyed a 20 per cent increase in four years and is projected to hit $66.3bn in 2028, despite fears within the industry that media rights growth has slowed and in some cases stopped.

“There is still growth out there, but it’s not being evenly spread among properties,” said SportBusiness Media editor Joseph Perry. 

“And what we found also is that, outside the top 10, every other sport is sharing one per cent of the media rights market. So there is more money being spent than ever, but it’s not being widely spread.”

While the top-line figure is up, the trend is for more of the money to flow to the biggest markets, sports and competitions, the report said.

US market, football and NFL lead ledia rights

The US makes up 54 per cent of media rights value in the top 10 markets and the figure is growing, thanks to the NBA and UFC renewals and the NFL’s world-leading contracts.

Football is the top driver of media rights, comprising 39 per cent of value generated by the top 10 sports, followed by American football. 

Of the top 10 competitions, the NFL’s $10bn-a-year package accounts for 19 per cent of total value, followed by the NBA’s $7bn and the Premier League’s $5bn.

The collapse of TV deals in French football and the relative struggles of the Italian and Spanish leagues to monetise an international audience has led to warnings about the direction of travel.

The Independent Football Regulator’s draft State of the Game report, published this week, noted that “the value of the next round of deals [for English clubs] is uncertain”.

“Competition organisers may face challenges when they next go to market,” it added. The IFR is chaired by former media rights executive David Kogan.

The Cherry Orchard at the Noel Coward Theatre with Kristin Scott Thomas and Stephen Mangan, review and star rating: ★★★★

Luminous Kristin Scott Thomas is the perfect choice for eccentric, blinkered stateswoman Lyubov Ranevskaya in Anton Chekhov’s The Cherry Orchard, a mound of gesticulating passion and nostalgic delusion as the broke matriarch being slowly and painfully dethroned from her Russian country pile. 

In the twentieth century’s first great play, written between 1901 and 1903, the aristocrats are fading from power against the rise of the upwardly mobile middle class, represented by Stephen Mangan’s self-made merchant, Yermolay Lopakhin. He is both a saviour and irritant to Ranevskaya in that he pitches to buy the family’s estate, but at the cost of sawing down the property’s prized cherry orchard and transforming the land into a series of smaller holiday homes.

The cherry orchard motif represents beauty and abundance, and Chekhov’s towering metaphor is intensified when contrasted with Chloe Lamford’s sparse set, the cold, crumbling opulence of a family drawing room in the house Ranevskaya is fighting to save.

Conor McPherson and Ian Rickson’s new adaptation leans into the script’s farcical elements. In particular, Rickson exploits Mangan’s comedic nose; at times his performance nears slapstick, but he carries a general effeteness and lightness of touch that makes him an interesting provocateur opposite the Four Weddings and a Funeral star’s airily out of touch matriarch.

The Cherry Orchard: a contemporary case

Chekhov’s secondary characters feel remarkably fleshed-out, even by today’s playwriting standards. Particularly strong are Ranevskaya’s daughter Anya and the academic, forward-thinking Petya, whose romanticising is hemmed in by their family duty.

Then there is 87-year-old servant Firs, the leading tragi-comedy figure whose ridiculous homages to old household furniture expose his dated value system, but whose vulnerable, genteel take on the famous act 2 outro brings a wonderful tenderness, even if the play’s final conceit feels flawed. To that end, the idea Firs represents in the final scene, that homeless people will be let down after the generous Ranevskaya moves out, doesn’t acknowledge the potential generosity of the new middle classes; in fact, people who have experienced poverty are often more likely to donate than those who haven’t.

As this bunch of nervous aristos raise a glass or five at what could be their final knees-up, it all hangs off of Scott Thomas, who feels birthed to deliver Chekhov’s profundities. “Maybe it is an illusion, but I’m as entitled to mine as you are to yours,” she gushes, and pitted against the backdrop of today’s ailing upper classes, Ranevskaya makes a brilliant, contemporary case.

The Cherry Orchard plays at the Harold Pinter Theatre until 9 January

Unlike conventional networking equipment, which relies heavily on electrical signals, the company’s optical circuit switching (OCS) technology keeps data travelling as light with the aim of reducing power consumption and delays. The approach could allow data centres to devote more of their limited electricity supply to running AI models rather than moving information between chips and servers.

“OCS will play a critical role in AI datacenter networking”, said Vaysh Kewada, chief executive and co-founder of Salience Labs. “As customers roll out optical links in their datacenters, high-performance optical switches are needed to deliver the token economics that workloads demand.”

The regulator has proposed tougher requirements for data centre developers to access the queue, including substantial upfront financial commitments, to prevent speculative projects from blocking access to the grid.

Ofcom has warned Elon Musk’s X it is still failing to effectively tackle illegal hate and terrorist content despite improvements in how quickly the platform responds to reports.

The UK watchdog said on Wednesday that X’s first quarterly performance report showed it was meeting agreed deadlines for reviewing suspected illegal material, but raised concerns about whether the content was actually being removed.

“We have ongoing concerns around the effectiveness of X’s response to taking down illegal hate and terror content”, Ofcom said.

The update comes as the regulator continues its investigation into X over the use of its Grok AI chatbot to generate and share sexualised deepfakes of real people, including children.

In May, X committed to reviewing suspected illegal hate and terrorist content reported through its dedicated UK reporting tool within an average of 24 hours. It also agreed to assess at least 85 per cent of reports within 48 hours over a three-month period.

Ofcom said X’s latest figures appeared to show improvements compared with evidence gathered earlier this year, with the platform meeting both targets.

However, the regulator said it would cross-check the figures against its own testing and expected X to maintain its performance.

It also reported mixed evidence about whether X was consistently working with independent experts to improve its moderation systems.

Ofcom expects to publish a further assessment early next year.

Grok investigation continues

The watchdog also provided an update on its investigation into Grok, launched in January after reports that the chatbot was being used to produce non-consensual sexual images of women and children.

Ofcom said it had gathered extensive evidence using its formal powers and was now assessing whether X had breached its duties under the Online Safety Act.

The investigation is looking into how X assessed the risks of illegal content appearing on its platform, whether users could easily report it and how the company handled moderation decisions.

If Ofcom finds reasonable grounds to believe X breached the law, it will issue provisional findings before giving the company an opportunity to respond.

The regulator also revealed that its investigation had uncovered circumstances in which pornography remained accessible to X accounts that had not been verified as belonging to adults.

X has since introduced changes to ensure content labelled as pornography is restricted to accounts that have completed its age verification checks.

The update comes amid growing tensions between the regulator and major tech companies over the implementation of Britain’s online safety laws.

X, Meta and Tiktok have recently challenged aspects of Ofcom’s information-gathering powers in court, while Meta has separately contested how the regulator calculates fees and penalties.

Under the Online Safety Act, companies found in breach of their duties can face fines of up to £18m or 10 per cent of qualifying worldwide revenue, whichever is greater.

As the automotive landscape shifts toward electrification, the global supercar market continues to be dragged, perhaps reluctantly, in the same direction, writes Tim Barnes-Clay.

Once ruled by raw mechanical power, modern supercars are increasingly judged on innovation, alternative fuels, and, in some cases, scarcity through limited production runs.

The 2026 Paris Motor Show, held at the French capital’s Expo Porte de Versailles, showcases these factors.

For high-net-worth collectors, the Alpine A310 Vision could be a future investment.

Until the Paris Motor Show, it was only known by its codename: PS1 (‘Projet Spécial 1’ – the missing ‘c’ in ‘Projet’ is not a misspelling).

As its codename suggests, Alpine discarded its rulebook when conceiving it.

Designed as a modern-day homage to the classic 1970s V6 A310 sports car, this new launch underscores Alpine’s ambition to create a range of ultra-exclusive, low-volume cars.

Drawing heavily on its experience as a Formula One constructor, the A310 Vision features F1-derived chassis dynamics and carbon-composite construction, aiming to whet the appetites of private collectors and motorsport purists.

Its launch is part of a bigger story, though: the French manufacturer’s debut of its new in-house ‘Special Projects’ division.

This department is designed for high-end models beyond the reach of most owners of Alpine’s mass-production vehicles.

With a decidedly modern take on a retro theme, the sharpened front end looks at home in the 2020s while strongly evoking a story from decades earlier.

Its space-age rear features a glowing Alpine ‘A’ badge, bulbous shoulders that exude muscular vibes, and the first letter in Alpine’s name even appears on its enormous alloy wheels as a dominant triangular pattern.

Denza is its new high-tech luxury offshoot brand, carrying the quality that has quickly earned BYD a steadfast reputation, with the Z Coupe among several new vehicles with excess power.

The Z Coupe produces an astonishing 1,603PS, capable of taking you from 0-62mph in a truly space-age 2.25 seconds.

Aesthetically, it blends McLaren, Porsche, and Ferrari, with a nod to its Far East roots in a rear end that hints at many a raucous Japanese performance car.

Denza may not have the brand recognition of Koenigsegg or Pagani, let alone Lamborghini or Ferrari. Still, the Z Coupe represents China’s biggest assault to date on Europe’s traditional supercar segment.

Linguistically, the ‘Tensei’ name certainly suggests Far Eastern origins and, indeed, means ‘rebirth’ or ‘reincarnation’ in Japanese, clearly signalling what’s to follow.

The Tensei is a reincarnation of the legendary Honda NSX, to the point that you’ll need to own an NSX to acquire a Tensei, because the latter is literally a rebodied version of the former, with your NSX serving as the donor car.

As improbable as its genesis may sound, the Tensei is poetry in motion, a revival of a long-lost era, and a love letter rewritten by a happy couple decades after it was first penned.

A simply beautiful combination of Japanese soul, British racing steel, and timeless Italian luxury design, presented in the howl of a V6 at 8,200rpm.

Luxury cinema chain Everyman is set to ditch its London listing for a private markets platform, after facing heavy pressure from key shareholders.

The London-headquartered group is set to join Asset Match’s Private Intermittent Securities and Capital Exchange System (Pisces) on 12 November, subject to shareholder approval on 30 October.

The move would make Everyman the first company to cancel its admission to Aim and opt to join a Pisces market.

The group said it intends to enable secondary trading on the platform, hosting periodic auctions where investors can buy or sell, ceasing the continuous trading that occurred on AIM. 

Iain Baillie, founder and executive chair of Asset Match, said: “It represents a significant moment for Pisces, demonstrating how the framework can support established consumer brands seeking a more flexible alternative to a traditional public listing.”

The group’s liquidity challenge

Hannah Woodley, commercial director of Asset Match, also wrote on LinkedIn that Everyman’s decision reflected the growing difficulty smaller companies face in raising money or trading shares on the stock market.

However, the cinema chain admitted it expects liquidity on Asset Match to be potentially lower than on Aim, with less frequent trading and less time for shareholders to assess their stock’s value between auction events.

Everyman’s inclusion makes it the second company to join Asset Match’s Pisces market, after British brewery Wadworth joined in August. Securing Everyman gives the platform a boost as it competes with the London Stock Exchange market, which boasts Wayve, Moneybox and Veremark.

Meanwhile, JP Jenkins has welcomed only one group under its framework so far, completing the transaction for digital board game maker Qplay in March. Vestd has yet to add a company to its framework.

Everyman turmoil

Everyman first announced in June that three of its directors, who together own nearly 46 per cent of its shares, favoured quitting London’s public market. 

The up-market cinema chain told shareholders this week that it believes its market value “does not reflect the positive achievements nor the underlying prospects of the business”. 

The firm said private ownership will help it take more drastic measures to ensure its survival amid a choppy period for the cinema industry, as it contends with intense competition from streaming services. 

Everyman said its financial performance can “change materially” each year, depending on the quality and number of films released. The resulting lack of accurate earnings guidance has “negatively impacted investor sentiment,” the firm said.

The group said it plans to shift its business model to rely less on ticket sales and more on corporate partnerships and private hire of its cinemas, as it targets annual revenue of £170m by the end of the decade.

This change in tack will leave Everyman exposed to a “period of volatility” in its performance, which could have threatened its share price if it remained on the public market, the firm said.

Online retail giant Wayfair is among three firms fined £6m by the competition watchdog for misleading sales tactics.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said on Wednesday it fined Wayfair £4.8m for misleading customers with false limited-time offers that did not end when they said they would.

This follows an investigation in which the CMA found products were advertised on Wayfair’s website through ‘Daily Deals’ and 24-hour ‘Flash Deals’, alongside messages such as ‘Here Today, Gone Tomorrow’ and countdown timers.

The competition watchdog’s probe found that many products remained available at the same price or lower after the stated deadline, meaning the time-limited offer was false.

“By stating these were one-day offers, people could have felt pressure to make a quick purchase so as not to lose out,” the CMA said.

Alongside Wayfair, the CMA fined home appliance retailer Appliances Direct £1.2m and ordered it to refund customers about £432,000, and City-based gym group Gold’s Gym, which was hit with a £45,000 fine and ordered to refund customers about £9,000.

The watchdog fined Appliance’s Direct for misleading time-limited offers, while it found Gold’s Gym failed to clearly list the total membership price, including the joining fee.

The chief executive of the appliance firm’s parent company, Buy It Direct Group, Nick Glynne, said in a post on LinkedIn the fine comes as “we fight the battle of our lives against an unprecedented wave of competition from Chinese traders, alongside rising employment costs, taxes and regulation.”

“Our controls were not adequate. But is this fine proportionate to the harm? In comparison, the average fine for corporate manslaughter is around £500,000,” Glynne said.

The competition watchdog said “all three parties engaged constructively with the CMA” and “admitted to breaking the law and agreeing to settle the case early with the CMA”, so they received a 40 per cent reduction in their fine.

“Whether buying a new sofa, a washing machine, or joining a gym, people should see genuine, accurate prices and offers – and decide for themselves whether they want optional extras. At a time when many households are carefully managing their budgets, people shouldn’t lose out because of misleading sales tactics,” Hayley Fletcher, senior director for consumer protection at the CMA, said.

“The time is up for this kind of behaviour. Businesses must treat their customers fairly and make sure they comply with the law, or risk hefty fines,” she added.

A Wayfair spokesperson said in a statement: “Although we believe the fine is excessive and disproportionate, we take the CMA’s findings seriously and we chose to settle so we can continue to focus on serving our customers.”

Gold’s Gym was contacted for comment.

In a letter to Sanderson’s board, LBV said the 26 per cent shareholder vote against the firm’s remuneration report at its annual meeting was “clear evidence of dissatisfaction among shareholders when it comes to board and executive compensation”.

Shareholder ‘baffled’ by threat

Patrick Lewis, who is an independent non-executive director and chair of Sanderson’s remuneration committee, wrote back to Emmanuel de Figueiredo, LBV’s founder, to warn him “the allegations contained in your letter have the potential to cause serious damage” to the group’s executives. 

In the letter, seen by City AM, he wrote: “My strong recommendation would be that you should not take any further steps to publish, circulate or repeat the allegations contained in your letter in their current form. 

“I expressly reserve all of our rights and remedies available to us, including the right to seek legal advice and pursue such action as may be appropriate in respect of any defamatory statements that are published. 

“I nevertheless hope that this will not be necessary and that any concerns raised by LBV can be addressed through proper and constructive engagement rather than through the publication of misleading and potentially defamatory allegations.”

Lewis has been a director at Sanderson since November 2021. Before joining the design group he served as finance chief of department store giant John Lewis, which he first joined in 1994.

‘They see us as troublemakers’

In LBV’s response to Lewis’s letter, de Figueiredo said it was “baffling” that he had interpreted his comments about Montague and Woodcock’s pay as “attacks on the executive management team”.

In the correspondence, the hedge fund boss wrote: “We categorically reject the characterisation in your letter that our comments amount, expressly or by implication, to an allegation that either executive is unsuitable for office and, therefore, defamatory or misleading in any way.”

LBV addressed Lewis’s threat in a circular sent to shareholders on Tuesday, saying: “A board that meets those legitimate views with the threat of legal action appears to believe its shareholders should not hold views of their own. They see us as troublemakers, rather than as stakeholders to be taken seriously.”

Sanderson’s investors have been called to an emergency meeting on 29 October to vote on LBV’s proposals to remove Dame Thompson and elect Stephen Brook as a director.

“LBV’s proposals risk significant disruption and uncertainty at precisely the point when the benefits of the group’s transformation are becoming increasingly evident,” Thompson has said to shareholders.

Sanderson Design Group and Lewis declined to comment.

The FTSE 250 self-storage provider jumped more than five per cent to 844p after Ancora Alternatives, which owns four per cent of the group, told it to consider a take-private deal.

The size of the British state is growing by a larger amount than any other G7 nation apart from Germany since the pandemic in 2020, figures on government spending from the International Monetary Fund have shown. 

The IMF’s latest report on countries’ fiscal outlook shows that UK government spending is set to rise by 5.2 percentage points between 2019 and 2031. 

This will make the size of the state rise to 43.3 per cent of GDP in 2030 compared to a level of just 38.1 per cent before Covid-19 dramatically changed the course of public finances. 

The US, France, Italy, Canada and Japan are projected to increase government spending by a smaller proportion as a share of their economies. France, Italy and Canada already spend more as a share of GDP. 

Germany is the only country among the seven dominant economies that is set to increase spending by a higher level. Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced last year that borrowing rules would be significantly loosened to fund 838 billion euros (more than £700bn) in mainly defence investment through to 2030. 

The fund’s report adds to anticipation ahead of Chancellor John Healey’s first budget, where he will be required to juggle spending pressures for the cost of living with limited scope against a difficult fiscal outlook.

Higher spending funded by huge tax rises

IMF forecasts also continued to project that the tax burden in the UK would grow at the fastest pace among advanced economies. 

Revenue as a share of GDP will come to about 41.9 per cent by 2031 following tax raids on businesses and households by the Labour government, rising from 38.2 per cent in 2025. 

Under current government plans, this would mean that the UK would go from having the second largest deficit in the G7, after only the US, in 2025 to posting the smallest one by 2031 at -1.4 per cent of GDP. 

IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva praised Labour ministers for taking “decisive” measures to limit borrowing as she said she thinks “the government recognises they need to stay the course”. On Wednesday, it was reported in the Financial Times that Chancellor John Healey would not raise borrowing in order to fund cost of living or business support, instead using tax hikes or spending cuts to fund proposals. 

However, IMF officials warned the Chancellor against raising the tax burden further to fund defence spending. 

Rodrigo Valdés, who leads the IMF’s research on fiscal policy, called for an “urgent” discussion about spending cuts when he was asked about how the UK could spend more on the military. 

“In general, Europe has relatively high revenue ratios. So the space for a lot more revenues is not easy,” he said. 

“[Tax] distorts at the end of the day, so the discussion about the social contract behind spending is very, very urgent in the sense that… less spending [will be] part of the new pressures that you will have from different sources.”

He added: “Debt spending will be very persistent. Defence spending will be persistent. So, even if you accommodate temporary risk with debt, you have to be prepared at some point to recognise that debt cannot forever finance this part.”

Should Andy Burnham call a snap election? Emily Sheffield reports from the political tittle tattle field of David Cameron’s 60th party in today’s Notebook

Party chat turns to politics at David Cameron’s 60th

This weekend in Cornwall, celebrating David Cameron’s 60th birthday, politics was refreshingly off the menu. This was all about family and old friends, cold water plunges, wind-blown hikes to shed hangovers and a lot of eating. Only once did talk briefly slip onto Westminster’s current obsession: will Andy Burnham hold a snap election.

The verdict from the politicos present was split. Most pinned spring 2027 as the likeliest date, not December; 2028 a strong possibility and 2029 the least likely. But everyone agreed that for Burnham the risks could still outweigh the gains, even if his advisors persuade him differently.

Firstly, what is his reason for the voting public about why he’s going to the polls? This was Theresa May’s mistake. She had none, then lost the sizable majority won by Cameron and never really recovered. Whereas Boris Johnson had a clear argument: Get Brexit Done. The polls point to Burnham being still short of a majority and losing 99 seats.

True, their ‘Lean Left’ strategy is working, so they could soon hit 30 per cent. But the public want PMs to get on with the job, polling can change fast in a fevered run-up. Let’s not forget Brenda from Bristol. When May called her snap election in April 2017, a reporter stopped Brenda in the street to break the news, and she replied, “You’re joking! Not another one! Oh, for God’s sake I can’t stand this!”

There is, of course, also a lesson in not calling one. Gordon Brown in 2007 let speculation about an autumn election build, then backed off, and “the election that never was” dogged him until 2010.

Soon speculation will lock Burnham in. Or risk him looking weak. More pressure for Chancellor John Healey to deliver on October 28.

Clarkson parties at The Savoy

Last Thursday, it was off to The Savoy for Jeremy Clarkson’s book launch, Diddly Squat, The G.O.A.T. We had bonded on stage at the farmer’s rally two years ago when 20,000 people gathered outside Westminster to protest at the family farms tax. And we’re still campaigning: Clarkson was in a suit for the second time that week, having wowed Conservative Party Conference on Monday. “But please don’t tell anyone you were here this evening,” he implored, “I forgot to ask 60 per cent of my friends, including all of my children!” Sorry Jezza, but you’re just a man we like to shout about.

Bayeux ticket wars continue

Finally, a viewing of the great Bayeux embroidery. First at a Bloomberg corporate event on Tuesday, where I slipped in as soon as the speeches ended and enjoyed a near solitary visit before the queue swelled. Then back the following day with our paid tickets for a 4.20pm slot. Two hours of queuing. I quit after one, leaving my husband who finally entered at 6.30pm, by which time all excitement had evaporated. British Museum, you do need to do better, or the frustration between the corporate and the public experience will grow far bigger.

Quote of the week

For people who say ‘Unite the right’ – we are not uniting with that

Kemi Badenoch on Reform

Kemi’s stylist

Huge kudos to fashion designer Polly McMaster, the founder and CEO of The Fold. Kemi Badenoch shone at the Tory Conference not just because of her speech, and sheer star quality, but also because of what she wore. And most of her stand-out outfits came from The Fold. For women in the City, The Fold is where they frequently turn because dressing for the boardroom and female leadership is surprisingly challenging. And McMaster is one of the few designers who has nailed it.

The man behind the mic

All broadcasters suffer a twinge of anxiety publicly airing our views. The reaction can be ferocious. The margin for error is wide. Frequently I have watched in amusement (or horror) as a comment of mine goes stratospheric on X or ends up on the front pages. And LBC broadcaster Iain Dale has drawn his fair share of controversy. So it is fitting that his memoir is entitled Have I Said Too Much? His books are on my shelves, and I regularly appear on his LBC panel sessions. Yet I know little of his life. This throws the door open.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

That per-capita figure is a calculation built on CB Insights’ data, not a ranking CB Insights itself publishes, and it is worth reading as a proxy for the ecosystem’s density rather than a formal league table.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Two decades later, in 2014, the government extended the same instinct outward with e-Residency, a digital identity scheme that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an Estonian company online, without granting them any right to actually live there. Neither programme produced a unicorn by itself. What they produced was a population that treated computers as ordinary tools a generation before most of Europe did, and a legal and administrative system built to let a small number of people start companies with very little friction.

The first of the ten billion-dollar companies was Skype, built in Tallinn in 2003. Its founders, the Swede Niklas Zennström and the Dane Janus Friis, co-founded the company with three Estonian engineers, Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn, who built the software behind what was then an unusually good way to make free voice calls over the internet. eBay bought the company two years later for a reported $2.6 billion in upfront cash and stock (total consideration including later earn-outs was reported as high as $4.1 billion).

Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

The clearest example of that inheritance is Wise. Its co-founder Taavet Hinrikus was Skype’s first employee; his eventual co-founder, Kristo Käärmann, worked at Deloitte in London. Both were Estonians living abroad with an ordinary, irritating problem: Hinrikus was paid in euros but lived in the UK, and Käärmann was paid in pounds but had a mortgage back in Estonia in euros. According to the company’s own account of its founding, on Wise’s own history page, the two of them started by simply swapping money directly with each other every month, at the real mid-market exchange rate, to avoid their banks’ fees and markups. They launched TransferWise, later renamed Wise, in 2011, and it went public in London a decade later, making both founders Estonia’s first tech billionaires.

That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. Estonian startups collectively reported €3.9 billion in revenue in 2024, up 14.7 percent on the year before, according to Invest in Estonia’s own sector figures, and the sector now employs about 14,400 people directly, or roughly one in every 38 working Estonians, at an average monthly salary of €3,650, more than double the national average. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

Milda Mitkutė was changing apartments in Vilnius in 2008 and had more clothes than the new place could hold. Rather than throw them out, she wanted a way to pass them on to people she knew. A friend, the software developer Justas Janauskas, built her a website for it. “We chatted about creating a website where people could trade their pre-loved fashion with each other,” Janauskas later told Tech.eu in 2015, recalling that he was doubtful the idea would go anywhere until he asked around and found most of his friends thought it was a good one.

What tipped it into something larger was almost accidental. A couch-surfing guest from Munich learned about the site, liked it, and helped carry the idea into Germany, where it launched under its own local name, Kleiderkreisel. Other country-specific spin-offs followed the same pattern for a few years, each with its own name and its own small user base, before the company folded them together under a single brand, Vinted, as the parent business decided a fragmented set of local sites made less sense than one platform users could recognise anywhere in Europe. The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing. Vinted makes its money almost entirely from the buyer’s side of the transaction: a fixed fee of roughly $0.70 plus a variable fee of about 5 percent of the item’s price, charged in the buyer’s local currency (figures as of late 2025) — according to Vinted’s own Buyer Protection fee page. That fee funds Vinted’s Buyer Protection service, including secure payment handling and dispute support. Shipping is a separate charge paid by the buyer at checkout, even though the seller receives a prepaid label. It is close to the inverse of how rivals like Poshmark and Depop have historically operated, charging the seller a cut instead. Underneath the fee structure sits a harder problem: getting a stranger’s old jumper from a seller’s flat to a buyer’s front door, cheaply and reliably, across dozens of countries. That has turned Vinted into as much a logistics company as a marketplace. It is worth naming the distinction because the two can look similar on a spreadsheet, and a 19 percent drop in profit reads very differently once it’s clear the company was profitable at all only two years earlier, and is still profitable now, just less so by design.

What the €10.8 billion figure represents is how far secondhand clothing has moved from a hobby into ordinary consumer behaviour across Europe. The company has said it intends to bring the same model to the United States next, according to Dealroom’s coverage of the 2025 results. Whether Vinted’s European logistics playbook, built over seventeen years and hundreds of thousands of parcel points, transfers to a market with a completely different postal and returns infrastructure is the open question the 2025 numbers don’t answer.

]]> Research suggests the brain doesn’t process scrolling through a feed like settling into a book — the constant change repeatedly asks attention to reset and decide what matters, which helps explain why an hour online can leave you feeling more mentally exhausted than informed https://siliconcanals.com/d-research-suggests-the-brain-doesnt-process-scrolling-through-a-feed-like-settling-into-a-book-every-new-post-asks-attention-to-reset-and-decide-what-matters-which-helps-explain-why-an-hour/ Sun, 20 Sep 2026 15:00:55 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109568

Rapidly changing feed content may increase task switching and decision-making, which can make scrolling feel mentally tiring.]]>

An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Where the tiredness comes from

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.
